learn.hook: Oersted showed currents make magnetism. Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry asked the reverse: can magnetism make a current? Their answer powers every home in India.
points: Electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field (more precisely, a changing magnetic flux) produces an emf and a current in a circuit.
It underlies generators in power plants, transformers, induction cooktops and wireless charging.
Experiment 1: moving a bar magnet towards or away from a coil connected to a galvanometer deflects it. Faster motion gives a larger deflection; no motion, no deflection.
Experiment 2: moving a current-carrying coil towards or away from a second coil induces a current in the second coil.
Experiment 3: with both coils stationary, switching the current in one coil on or off induces a brief current in the other. A steady current induces nothing.

example.q: A magnet is held still inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. What does the galvanometer show? What if the magnet is pulled out quickly?
steps: Stationary magnet: flux through the coil is constant, so no emf.
Pulling it out changes the flux quickly.
example.answer: No deflection when still; a large deflection while it is pulled out quickly

learn.reallife: Every unit of electricity reaching Indian homes from Bhakra Nangal, Tehri or NTPC's coal plants is produced by electromagnetic induction in giant generators.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can I get electricity just by putting a magnet near a coil?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Only a changing flux induces an emf, so the magnet or coil must move, or the current must change. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good! Is a magnet resting near the coil enough? What must happen?

learn.hook: All of Faraday's experiments had one thing in common: the number of magnetic field lines through the coil was changing. Physicists call it magnetic flux.
points: Faraday's conclusion: an induced emf appears whenever the magnetic flux through a circuit changes.
Magnetic flux through a plane area A in a uniform field: Φ = B·A = BA cosθ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area.
For a non-uniform field: Φ = Σ B·dA (sum over small elements).
Flux is a scalar. SI unit: weber (Wb), 1 Wb = 1 T m².
Flux can be changed in three ways: change B, change the area A, or change the angle θ (rotate the coil).

example.q: A square loop of side 10 cm is in a field of 0.5 T, with its normal at 60° to B. Find Φ.

learn.reallife: Induction cooktops sold across India change the magnetic flux through the pan's base 20,000 or more times a second, so currents swirl in the metal and heat it.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly is magnetic flux, and how can I change it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Φ = BA cosθ, so change B, A or θ to change the flux. Three knobs to turn!
teach.nudge: Good! Write the formula for flux. Which three quantities can change it?

learn.hook: The emf you get does not depend on how much flux there is, but on how fast it changes. Faraday turned that idea into a law with one simple equation.
points: Faraday's law: the induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt.
For a coil of N turns: ε = -N dΦ/dt. Average emf ε = -NΔΦ/Δt.
Induced current I = ε/R, and the charge that flows Q = NΔΦ/R (independent of how fast the change happens).
Example: pulling a square loop out of a field region changes Φ from BA to 0; the emf depends on how quickly it is removed.
The minus sign expresses Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change.

example.q: A 50-turn coil of area 0.02 m² is perpendicular to a field that drops from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.2 s. Find the average emf.
steps: ΔΦ per turn = ΔB × A = 0.4 × 0.02 = 8 × 10⁻³ Wb

learn.reallife: Electromagnetic flow meters used by Indian water utilities measure flow speed from the emf induced in moving water as it crosses a magnetic field, a direct use of Faraday's law.

quiz.q: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction is written as
quiz.explain: Induced emf equals minus the rate of change of flux linkage.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Does a stronger magnet always give more induced voltage?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It is the rate of change of flux, times the number of turns, that sets the emf. A still magnet gives nothing!
teach.nudge: Good! What exactly does the emf depend on according to Faraday's law?

learn.hook: Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and it falls in eerie slow motion. Lenz's law is pushing back.
points: Lenz's law: the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
This is a consequence of conservation of energy: you must do work against the opposing force, and that work becomes electrical energy (and heat).
If the induced current helped the change, energy would appear from nothing, which is impossible.
Magnet's N pole approaching a coil: the coil's near face becomes a north pole (repels). N pole moving away: the near face becomes south (attracts).
A loop leaving a field region: the induced current tries to keep the flux, so its own field is in the same direction as the external field.

example.q: A magnet's north pole is pushed towards a coil. Seen from the magnet's side, what is the direction of the induced current?
steps: The coil opposes it by making its near face a north pole.
A north face, seen from outside, has an anticlockwise current.
example.answer: Anticlockwise, as seen from the magnet's side

learn.reallife: Electromagnetic brakes on some metro trains, like Delhi Metro's regenerative systems, use induction: the induced currents oppose the motion, slowing the train and feeding energy back to the grid.

games.title: Lenz logic
items: The induced current always opposes the change in flux.
That is Lenz's law.
Lenz's law follows from conservation of charge.
It follows from conservation of energy.
When a north pole approaches a coil, the near face of the coil becomes a south pole.
It becomes north, to repel.
Work done against the opposing force appears as electrical energy.
Energy is conserved.
A magnet dropped through a copper pipe falls more slowly than in free fall.
Induced currents in the pipe oppose its motion.

quiz.q: A north pole of a magnet moves away from a coil. The face of the coil nearest the magnet becomes a
quiz.explain: The coil opposes the decrease in flux by trying to hold the magnet back.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coil always repels

quiz.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
quiz.explain: Opposing the change means work must be done, which becomes electrical energy.
quiz.mistake: Links it with charge conservation

quiz.q: A rectangular loop is being pulled out of a region of uniform field pointing into the page. The induced current in the loop flows

quiz.explain: Inward flux is falling, so the loop makes its own inward field: clockwise current (right-hand rule).
quiz.mistake: Opposes the field instead of the change in flux

quiz.q: What would happen if the induced current aided the change in flux instead of opposing it?
options: The current would be very small
Energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy
quiz.explain: A self-reinforcing change would grow without any work input, which is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the energy argument

quiz.q: A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls slowly because
options: currents induced in the tube oppose its motion (Lenz's law)
air resistance in the tube is high
quiz.explain: As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring of the tube changes, inducing currents whose magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law).
quiz.mistake: Thinks copper is magnetic

quiz.q: The field through a loop points upward and is increasing. The induced current produces a field that, inside the loop, points
quiz.explain: To oppose the increase of upward flux, the induced field points down.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pushing a magnet into a coil requires more effort when the coil's ends are joined than when they are open. Reason (R): With the ends joined, an induced current flows and opposes the motion. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With an open circuit there is an emf but no current, so no opposing magnetic force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the emf alone exerts the force

quiz.q: A metal ring is placed around the top of a vertical solenoid. When the current in the solenoid is switched on, the ring

quiz.explain: The increasing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes it, so the ring is repelled (the jumping ring experiment).
quiz.mistake: Thinks induced currents always attract

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the induced current always fight the change? Is it just being stubborn?'
teach.praise: Chirp! If it helped, energy would come from nowhere. Opposing the change keeps energy conserved: work in, electricity out!
teach.nudge: Good! Which conservation law would be broken if the induced current helped the change?

learn.hook: Slide a metal rod across two rails in a magnetic field and a voltage appears between its ends, no battery needed. It is the simplest generator possible.
points: A rod of length l moving at speed v perpendicular to a uniform B, on rails forming a loop: area changes at rate lv, so ε = Blv.
Explanation with Lorentz force: each free charge in the rod feels qvB along the rod, pushing charges to one end; the work per unit charge over length l is vBl.
If the circuit has resistance R, current I = Blv/R flows, and the rod feels a retarding force F = BIl = B²l²v/R.
To keep the rod at constant speed, an external force must supply power P = Fv = B²l²v²/R, which equals the electrical power I²R dissipated. Energy is conserved.
The direction of the induced current can be found by Fleming's right-hand rule or by Lenz's law.

example.q: A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.2 T field on rails with R = 2 Ω. Find ε, I and the force needed.

learn.reallife: When a Vande Bharat train speeds along, its steel axle is a long conductor moving through Earth's magnetic field, so a small motional emf exists between the ends of the axle.

topics.title: Rotating rods, wheels and moving vehicles

learn.hook: An aeroplane's metal wings, a spinning bicycle wheel and a train's axle all cut Earth's magnetic field. Each one is a tiny, unintended generator.
points: A metal rod of length l rotating with angular speed ω about one end, perpendicular to B: different parts move at different speeds (v = ωr). Total ε = ½Bωl².
A metal wheel spinning in an axial field has the same emf between its centre (axle) and rim: ε = ½BωR².
A plane flying horizontally: its wings cut the vertical component of Earth's field, so ε = B_vertical × wingspan × speed.
A train moving on level tracks: its axle (length l) cuts the vertical component, so ε = B_vertical × l × v.
Exercise toolkit: ε = -NdΦ/dt, ε = Blv, ε = ½Bωl², ε = -L dI/dt and ε = -M dI/dt.

example.q: A 0.8 m metal rod rotates at 250 rad s⁻¹ about one end in a field of 0.4 T along its axis of rotation. Find the emf between its ends.

learn.reallife: A passenger jet with a 34 m wingspan flying at 250 m s⁻¹ over north India, where the vertical component of Earth's field is about 3 × 10⁻⁵ T, has roughly 0.26 V across its wingtips. It cannot drive a current because the whole plane moves together.

learn.hook: Wireless phone chargers, Indian Railways track circuits and every transformer rely on one coil 'talking' to another through changing flux. That link is mutual inductance.
points: For a coil near a current, flux linkage NΦ is proportional to the current. The constant of proportionality is the inductance.
Inductance depends only on the geometry of the coils (turns, size, separation) and the medium (permeability). SI unit: henry (H), 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹.
Mutual inductance: N₁Φ₁ = M₁₂I₂, the flux in coil 1 due to current in coil 2. It can be shown that M₁₂ = M₂₁ = M.
Two long coaxial solenoids (inner radius r₁, length l, turns per metre n₁ and n₂): M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l. With a core of µr, M is multiplied by µr.
Induced emf in one coil due to changing current in the other: ε₁ = -M dI₂/dt.

example.q: Two coils have M = 0.2 H. The current in coil 2 rises from 0 to 5 A in 0.1 s. Find the emf in coil 1.

learn.reallife: Wireless chargers for phones sold in Indian markets put a transmitter coil and a receiver coil close together; the larger their mutual inductance, the better the charging.

The mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 equals that of coil 2 with respect to coil 1.
M₁₂ = M₂₁.
Moving two coils further apart reduces their mutual inductance.
Less flux links them.
A steady current in one coil induces a steady emf in the other.

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: This reciprocity holds generally, so the induced emf per unit rate of change is the same both ways.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger coil always has a larger M

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a current in one coil create a voltage in another coil that it does not touch?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A changing current in one coil changes the flux through the other, inducing ε = -M dI/dt. No touching needed!
teach.nudge: Good! What must be changing, and what quantity links the two coils?

topics.title: Self-inductance and energy in an inductor

learn.hook: Switch off a large motor and you may see a spark at the switch. The coil fights the sudden drop in its own current with a burst of back emf.
points: Self-inductance: a coil's own flux linkage NΦ = LI. Changing I induces an emf in the same coil: ε = -L dI/dt (back emf).
The back emf opposes any change in current, rising or falling. An inductor plays the role in circuits that mass (inertia) plays in mechanics.
Long solenoid of n turns per metre, area A and length l: L = µ₀n²Al. With a core: L = µrµ₀n²Al.
Energy stored in an inductor: U = ½LI², analogous to kinetic energy ½mv².

Mutual inductance examples: for long coaxial solenoids M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l; for a small loop of radius r₁ at the centre of a large coplanar loop of radius r₂ (r₁ ≪ r₂), the large loop's field µ₀I/(2r₂) is nearly uniform over the small loop, so M = µ₀πr₁²/(2r₂).

example.q: A 0.5 H inductor carries 4 A. Find the stored energy. If the current falls to zero in 0.01 s, what average back emf appears?

learn.reallife: Tube lights in older Indian homes used a choke (an inductor). Its large back emf when the starter opened gave the high voltage spike needed to strike the tube.

quiz.q: The current in a 0.3 H coil changes at 50 A s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the self-induced emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Divides L by dI/dt

quiz.q: An inductor of 2 H carries 3 A. How much energy is stored in it (in J)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ or the square

quiz.q: A solenoid has 1000 turns per metre, cross-section 10⁻³ m² and length 0.5 m. What is its self-inductance (in mH)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷, π = 3.14)
quiz.mistake: Uses n instead of n²

quiz.q: The number of turns per unit length of a solenoid is doubled (same size). Its self-inductance becomes
quiz.explain: L ∝ n².
quiz.mistake: Thinks L ∝ n

quiz.q: A small circular loop of radius r₁ lies at the centre of a much larger coplanar circular loop of radius r₂ (r₁ ≪ r₂). What is their mutual inductance?
quiz.explain: A current I in the large loop gives B = µ₀I/(2r₂) at its centre, almost uniform over the small loop. Flux through the small loop = πr₁² × µ₀I/(2r₂), so M = Φ/I = µ₀πr₁²/(2r₂).
steps: Field at centre of large loop: B = µ₀I/(2r₂)
Flux through small loop: Φ = B × πr₁² = µ₀Iπr₁²/(2r₂)
quiz.mistake: Uses the area of the large loop instead of the small loop, or forgets the factor 2 in the loop-centre field

quiz.q: A coil's current rises from 0 to 2 A in 0.05 s, and the average back emf is 8 V. What is L (in H)?
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: Why does a spark often appear at a switch when the current in a large inductive coil is suddenly cut?
options: The coil stores charge like a capacitor
The switch has very high resistance
The rapid fall in current induces a large back emf that opposes the drop
quiz.explain: |ε| = L dI/dt is large when dI/dt is large.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an inductor with a capacitor

quiz.q: An inductor's role in a circuit is analogous to which quantity in mechanics?
quiz.explain: It resists changes in current as mass resists changes in velocity.
quiz.mistake: Links it with friction

quiz.q: The energy stored in an inductor is 8 J when the current is 2 A. What is the energy when the current is 4 A (in J)?
quiz.explain: U ∝ I²: doubling I gives 4 × 8 = 32 J.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the energy instead of quadrupling

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a coil push back when I try to change its current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A changing current changes the coil's own flux, inducing a back emf -L dI/dt that opposes the change. Like inertia!
teach.nudge: Good! What does a coil induce in itself when its current changes, and which way does it act?

learn.hook: At Tehri dam, falling water spins turbines that turn huge coils in magnetic fields. The flux through each coil swings back and forth 50 times every second.
points: Principle: a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field has a continuously changing flux Φ = NBA cos ωt.
Induced emf ε = NBAω sin ωt. Peak emf ε₀ = NBAω; it is zero when the coil's plane is perpendicular to B and maximum when the plane is parallel to B.
Construction: armature coil, strong field magnets, slip rings that rotate with the coil, and carbon brushes that press on the rings to take the current out.
In hydroelectric plants, falling water turns the turbines; in thermal plants, steam does it. The generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
India's mains frequency is 50 Hz, so ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad s⁻¹.

example.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.05 m² rotates at 50 rev s⁻¹ in a 0.02 T field. Find the peak emf. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: The grid frequency monitored by Grid-India stays very close to 50 Hz; if generators slow down under heavy load, the frequency dips and control centres respond in seconds.

When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field

quiz.q: A generator converts

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a spinning coil make alternating current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! As the coil spins, the flux changes as cos ωt, so the emf is NBAω sin ωt, flipping direction every half turn. AC!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the flux as the coil rotates, and what shape is the emf?
